crises (2), By Ayo Akerele by Ayo Akerele November 10, 2026 Reading Time: 9 mins read 0 Add us on Google
One of the most profound and often misunderstood dimensions of entering new seasons is the reality of injuries. Many believers assume that injuries are always signs of failure, carelessness, or spiritual weakness. But Scripture reveals that injuries can be part of God’s preparation, part of His breaking process, part of His refining work, and part of His strategy for elevation.
Jacob’s injury at Peniel is one of the most powerful illustrations of this truth. The angel dislocated Jacob’s hip, yet this injury did not disqualify him. Instead, it marked him, humbled him, and prepared him for his new identity. Not every injury is caused by carelessness. Not every injury is caused by sin.
Some injuries are divinely permitted to break self ‑ dependence and force reliance on God.
Below are the major categories of injuries believers experience on the way to new seasons — each one preserved from your original teaching and expanded for depth and clarity.
These are injuries caused by lack of discernment, foolishness, impatience, or emotional decisions. They include:
These losses can bite deeply. They can create emotional wounds, financial pain, and spiritual discouragement.
Follow us on Google News and never miss breaking stories, investigations, and in-depth reporting.
Lot in Genesis 13 made a wrong choice — choosing the land that looked fertile but was spiritually dangerous. His decision led to severe injuries: loss of property, loss of peace, loss of security, and near loss of his family.
Yet even these losses can be part of God’s preparation. They teach discernment. They teach humility. They teach dependence on God rather than sight.
Joseph experienced this injury. Imagine how many people in Egypt heard that Joseph attempted to rape Potiphar’s wife. His reputation was destroyed. His name was stained. His future seemed ruined.
Yet Joseph’s injury was part of his preparation. God used defamation to reposition him. The injury did not stop his new season — it ushered him into it.
This injury is extremely serious because it comes from people you trust:
David endured this injury for thirteen years under Saul. Saul’s jealousy produced relentless attacks. David lost peace, stability, and safety. He lived as a fugitive. Yet David refused to fight back. He refused to retaliate. He refused to avenge himself.
If David had fought Saul, he might have missed his new season. Wisdom preserved him.
Betrayal is one of the deepest injuries. It destroys trust. It wounds the soul. It creates emotional scars. Daniel experienced betrayal from political colleagues who envied his rising influence. Their betrayal led to the lions’ den — yet it also led to Daniel’s promotion.
Betrayal is often a sign that you are close to a new season. It reveals hearts. It exposes motives. It separates you from wrong alliances.
Some injuries are consequences of disobedience. Others are permitted by God to train, discipline, and refine His people.
This is the most mysterious category. It occurs when God Himself allows or initiates an injury to break pride, self ‑ dependence, or fleshly confidence.
Jacob’s dislocated hip was not punishment — it was preparation. God broke Jacob to rebuild Israel. Divine breaking is painful, but it is purposeful. It empties you of dependence on men and forces you to lean on God alone.
Section 6: How to Endure, Persevere, and Win Despite Injuries
Perseverance is essential. Injuries do not disqualify you. They refine you. They strengthen you. They prepare you. Jacob persevered despite his injury. He refused to let go. He held on to the angel and demanded a blessing.
This is one of the most difficult instructions. When injured, the flesh wants to retaliate, defend, avenge, and justify itself. But Scripture teaches:
Injuries can cloud judgment. Pain can distort perception. Hurt can produce fleshly decisions. Therefore:
Never make strategic decisions in the flesh. Injuries require spiritual clarity.
Jacob’s final battle was not about strength, strategy, or endurance. It was about identity. The angel asked:
This was not a question of information. The angel already knew Jacob’s name. It was a question of revelation. It was a question of confrontation. It was a question of transformation.
This identity could not enter the new season. God wanted a nation, not a trickster. God wanted Israel, not Jacob. Before God could elevate Jacob, He had to confront Jacob’s identity.
Many believers today are crying for new seasons, but heaven does not recognize them. Their names are not written.
Their identities are not aligned. Their hearts are not transformed.
Jesus asked, “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered correctly. Jesus changed his name and moved him into a new season.
Jesus asked, “What is your name?” Identity was confronted before deliverance.
Jacob admitted his identity. God changed his name to Israel.
Your original teaching listed thirteen name changes — nine by God for good, four by pagan systems for evil. This section is preserved and expanded with theological commentary.
Section 8: Three Modern Examples of Believers Who Rose Despite Losses, Injuries and Identity Crises
Nicky Cruz grew up in a home filled with witchcraft, violence, and rejection. His identity was shaped by brutality and gang life. He suffered emotional injuries, abandonment, and deep trauma. Yet when he encountered Christ through David Wilkerson, he repented and surrendered. Despite the injuries of his past—crime, hatred, and a destroyed reputation—God transformed him into a global evangelist. His life proves that even the most shattered identity can be reborn into a powerful new season.
Joyce Meyer — From Abuse and Shame to International Ministry
Joyce Meyer endured years of sexual abuse, emotional injuries, and a deeply damaged identity. Her early adulthood was marked by fear, anger, and brokenness. Yet through repentance, healing, and perseverance, she rose into a new season. Today she leads one of the largest Christian teaching ministries in the world. Her life demonstrates that God can elevate anyone who refuses to let injuries define their destiny.
John Newton lived with a dark identity — slave trader, immoral, rebellious. After surviving storms, losses, and near death, he repented and surrendered to Christ. Despite the injuries of guilt and a ruined reputation, God transformed him into a pastor and the author of Amazing Grace. His life shows that repentance can rewrite even the most negative identity into a legacy of greatness.
Many believers today are standing at the 11th hour of their transition. Heaven has written their new season, but heaven is waiting for them. Waiting for repentance. Waiting for identity alignment. Waiting for surrender. Waiting for transformation.
God is calling His people into new seasons, but He is also calling them into new identities. The question is the same today as it was at Peniel:
